Power & utilities · Zimbabwe

Structures and vegetation inside power-line wayleaves, mapped and dated

Zimbabwe’s Electricity (Public Safety) Regulations set a wayleave clearance for every voltage, measured either side of the outermost conductor, and require licensees to keep trees from encroaching on conductors. We measure each structure’s distance to your line and to the wayleave edge, group the results by span or 500 m stretch, and show what is new since the last survey. Satellite first, and a person reviews every result.

Send us your line route See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

What changes under the line between patrols

“Homes and stalls keep appearing under our lines.”

The regulations bar structures, business activity and farming inside the wayleave clearance. Each new structure is a safety risk, a maintenance-access problem and a harder conversation once someone lives or trades in it.

“Trees are growing into the conductors.”

Licensees must make sure that no trees or foliage grow to the point of encroaching on and interfering with supply conductors (S.I. 177 of 2018, s.9(3)). Knowing which spans have regrown tells the clearing crews where to go.

“Someone has been digging near our cable route.”

Anyone digging, boring, trenching or breaking ground must first get the location of underground cables from the licensee (s.8). Fresh earthworks near a route where nobody asked are worth a visit.

“Our towers and cables are being damaged.”

Imagery cannot see theft, vandalism or who was near a tower. It can show fresh digging, new tracks and cleared ground near towers, so patrols know where to look.

Who this is for

  • Wayleave and servitude officers
  • Transmission and distribution asset teams
  • Line maintenance and vegetation-clearing supervisors
  • GIS and network-records teams
  • Land and ESIA teams on new lines
  • Solar and grid-connection project teams
  • EPC contractors and their E&S consultants

The clearances

The S.I. 177 wayleave clearances, and the mining setbacks beside them

The Electricity (Public Safety) Regulations, 2018 (S.I. 177 of 2018) set the clearances in their Fourth Schedule, “Wayleave Clearance (m) either side from the outermost conductor”. No one may place an object, carry on a business or activity, farm or erect a structure inside them (s.9(1)). Placing an object or erecting a structure closer needs the written authorisation of the distributor responsible for the energised conductor (s.9(2)), and a contravention carries a fine of up to level 5 (S.I. 177 of 2018).

Voltage Wayleave No mining
11 and 22 kV 5 m 10 m
33 kV 7.5 m 10 m
66 and 88 kV 15 m 25 m
132 kV 15 m 25 m
330 and 400 kV 30 m 40 m

The two columns are measured differently. The wayleave clearance (S.I. 177, Fourth Schedule) runs either side of the outermost conductor, so the strip on the ground depends on the tower or pole geometry; we work from your conductor positions, your tower types or your wayleave polygons rather than a single width from the centre line. The Mines and Minerals Act’s setback (s.34(8)), within which no prospecting or mining may take place, runs from the centre line, and the Act adds 10 m around pole- or ground-mounted transformers under 300 kVA and 25 m around other transformers, substations and electrical equipment or buildings (Mines and Minerals Act). Where a line crosses a mining location, see mining locations in Zimbabwe.

Checked 27 September 2026

The clearances were read from the gazetted page of S.I. 177 of 2018, whose Arrangement of Sections calls the table the Third Schedule. The Electricity Act’s own provisions on wayleave acquisition were not available to us, so we do not summarise them. This is a summary, not legal advice.

Existing lines

A register of what stands in the wayleave, then what changed

We buffer your line in its UTM zone at the clearance for its voltage, or at the wayleave polygons you send, and list each structure the review confirms with its distance to the line, its distance to the wayleave edge, its span or chainage and its coordinates. Cleared and cultivated ground inside the clearance is shown as its own layer, because s.9(1) bars farming in the wayleave as well as building.

Each 500 m stretch, or each span if you send tower positions, is rated for encroachment density, high, medium or low, by a count rule. The rating is a way to plan visits, not a safety rating.

Lines are then re-surveyed on a schedule you agree with us. New and removed structures between dated surveys are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views, and your team receives a notice after each survey saying what changed and where. Around substations, the line becomes a site boundary: we list what stands inside it and in a ring around it.

What you receive

  • A wayleave register: ID, distance to the line and to the wayleave edge, span or chainage, coordinates
  • Cleared and cultivated ground inside the clearance
  • A density rating for each span or 500 m stretch
  • New and removed structures between surveys, with before-and-after views
  • A change notice after each survey
  • A PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

At handover. Under regulations gazetted on 31 July 2026, land developers build the medium- and low-voltage backbone for their developments at their own cost and transfer it at no cost to the primary distribution licensee, and ZETDC is defined as “the sole owner of electricity backbone infrastructure in Zimbabwe” (S.I. 128 of 2026, ss.5–6). A dated register of what stands inside the wayleave on the day a network is handed over records what the licensee took on.

Buried cables

Fresh digging near your underground routes

Before “digging, boring, trenching, grading, excavating or breaking ground”, a contractor, owner or occupant must get the location of underground cables from the licensee and use a cable avoidance tool. Licensees keep maps of their networks, and cables are laid in designated servitudes or, where that is not possible, on clearly marked routes (S.I. 177 of 2018, s.8).

That rule depends on people asking. Between surveys we flag fresh excavation, trenches, spoil and earthworks visible at the surface within the distance you set from your cable routes, each located and dated, so your teams can check whether the work was notified. Only surface works are visible: a cable or a joint under the ground is not.

What this layer is

  • Fresh digging and earthworks near the routes you send
  • The imagery date on which each first appears
  • Flagged for your teams to check, never a finding

Excavation and ground-disturbance mapping

Vegetation and fire

Where spans have regrown, been cleared or burnt

The regulations make licensees keep trees and foliage from interfering with conductors, let them clear vegetation outside the wayleave that is likely to interfere, de-energising first, and forbid anyone to stop them (s.9(3)–(6)). Under an amendment gazetted on 31 July 2026, “wayleave clearing”, substation weeding and general clearing around electrical infrastructure are excluded from the maintaining-or-repairing limb of “electrical works”, provided a competent electrical artisan or linesman supervises (S.I. 121 of 2026, Fifth Schedule).

Cleared and regrown vegetation

Where vegetation along each span has been cleared or has grown back between dates, from Copernicus Sentinel data, so clearing crews can plan by span. It shows larger patches of change, not individual trees.

Fire near the line

Satellite-detected fire hotspots from NASA FIRMS near the lines you name, checked by a reviewer, then maps of the burnt area. Not an emergency or early-warning service: small, short-lived or cloud-covered fires can be missed.

Before and after clearing

Dated scenes either side of a clearing campaign, so the record shows which spans were cleared and when, next to the structure register.

Vegetation, land cover and fire, in detail

New lines, grid connections and rehabilitation

Count what stands on the route before it is fixed

High-voltage transmission lines are First Schedule projects under the Environmental Management Act and need an EMA certificate before they are built (s.97). Lender-financed work adds its own requirements. Terms of reference published in Zimbabwe in May 2026 for lender-funded solar site studies, which include the right of way for the grid connection, ask, where a resettlement action plan is needed, for cut-off dates, the approximate number of affected structures, photographs and GIS coordinates of each potentially affected entity, and the use of aerial photos and satellite imagery, and for the topographic survey to be signed off by a qualified land surveyor.

For a new line or connection we compare the structures along alternative alignments, screen slope, drainage crossings and flood exposure, and pull the imagery history of contested parcels. Once the route is fixed, a dated register supports landowner engagement and the cut-off-date records; it does not replace the census or stand in for the topographic survey.

Rehabilitation programmes change the network too: the Ministry of Energy and Power Development reports AfDB-funded rehabilitation of transmission and distribution in the Midlands and Manicaland (Ministry, December 2025). A baseline taken before the works, and a survey after them, show what changed inside the wayleave.

Route and cut-off baselines

  • Structure counts along each alternative alignment
  • Slope, drainage and flood screening of the route
  • A dated register on the cut-off date
  • What appeared after it, between surveys

Drones along a line

Where a span needs more detail than satellite shows

Drone surveys are subject to the CAAZ approvals and security clearances each operation requires. Along a line that usually means an operator whose certificate covers the planned flights, the asset owner’s permission to fly within 30 m of towers, poles and substations (S.I. 271 of 2018, s.43), approval to fly over, along or within 30 m of a public road (s.44), approval for any leg beyond the pilot’s sight (s.40), and CAAZ approval for flights adjacent to or above a national key point or strategic installation (s.39(3)). Afridrone is working towards the approvals Zimbabwe requires; every drone proposal names the company that will fly and its approvals.

If your own team or a contractor already flies your lines, send the orthophotos or GeoTIFFs. We run the same register, change and vegetation analysis on them, a person reviews every result, and dated satellite scenes fill the gaps between flights.

How it works

From line route to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route, tower positions, voltages and any wayleave polygons, and say what the register is for: maintenance, vegetation, a handover, a new route or a cut-off date. The bands, imagery and deliverables go into a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures and ground change are mapped along the whole line from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos you hold.

  3. Look closer where needed

    Your own flights, or drone surveys where the approvals allow, cover the spans that need detail.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result; structures are measured against the clearance, stretches are rated, and the report and GIS layers go to the contacts you name.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, cultivated and cleared ground, fresh excavation and tracks visible from the air
  • Measure each structure to the line and to the S.I. 177 clearance or your wayleave polygons
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Deliver dated records that support your wayleave, engagement and legal processes

What we don’t do

  • Measure conductor clearance, sag or tower condition
  • See buried cables, theft or vandalism, or say who did anything
  • Identify, count or follow people
  • Carry out land surveys, or decide whether a structure is authorised

Frequently asked questions

What is the wayleave distance for a 330 kV line in Zimbabwe?

30 m either side of the outermost conductor, the same as for 400 kV (S.I. 177 of 2018, Fourth Schedule). Because the distance is measured from the outermost conductor, not the centre line, the strip on the ground is wider than 60 m by the spread of the conductors on the tower. Placing an object or erecting a structure closer needs the distributor’s written authorisation (s.9(2)).

How far from a power line can I build in Zimbabwe?

Outside the wayleave clearance for the line’s voltage, measured either side of the outermost conductor: 5 m for 11 kV and 22 kV, 7.5 m for 33 kV, 15 m for 66, 88 and 132 kV, and 30 m for 330 and 400 kV (S.I. 177 of 2018). Placing an object or erecting a structure closer is allowed only with the distributor’s written authorisation (s.9(2)). For a particular plot, ask the distributor responsible for the line, and before digging anywhere, ask the licensee where its underground cables run (s.8).

Is farming allowed under power lines?

Not within the wayleave clearance. Section 9(1) of S.I. 177 of 2018 bars anyone from placing an object, carrying on any business or activity, farming or erecting a structure within the prescribed clearance. The distributor’s written authorisation under s.9(2) covers placing an object or erecting a structure closer, not farming. The regulations also allow for vegetation to be cleared where it interferes with the conductors.

Can you measure the clearance to our conductors?

No. We show where structures, cultivated ground and vegetation change sit in the wayleave and how far each is from the line. Conductor heights, sag and ground clearance stay with your line engineers, and none of our layers is a measured clearance.

Do you detect cable theft or tower vandalism?

No. Satellites cannot see theft, vandalism or who was near a tower. We flag land change at the surface, such as fresh digging, spoil, new tracks and cleared ground near towers and cable routes, so your teams know where to check first.

How close can mining come to a power line?

The Mines and Minerals Act bars prospecting and mining within 10 m of the centre line of a line of 33 kV or less, 25 m of lines above 33 kV and up to 132 kV, and 40 m of lines above 132 kV, with 10 m or 25 m setbacks from transformers, substations and other electrical equipment (s.34(8)). We flag new pits, spoil and cleared ground inside those bands between surveys.

Send us your line route

KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, with tower positions and the voltage of each line or section, and the wayleave polygons if you hold them. Tell us if your team already flies the line. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
